 Actions demanded on prices, wages, housing 
 Ideas & Opinions — Darrell Berkheimer: Actions demanded on prices, wages, housing 
 Darrell Berkheimer | Columnist 
 Nov 14, 2026

 Ending the Iran war and ending the tariffs will lower prices some — slowly. But don’t expect the prices to drop to anywhere near what they were before the tariffs and war.
 Once prices are raised — for whatever the temporary situations might be — they never retract to what they were before the changes bumped them upward.
 That means workers also will need increases in wages and salaries — even more than the affordability and inequality increases they needed prior to the tariffs and war.
 The national minimum wage remains at $7.25. And our young folks might remark that cap was set back in the “middle ages” of 2009.
 Somewhat fortunately, California’s minimum wage – currently at $16.90 – is scheduled to increase 50 cents to $17.40 this coming Jan. 1, based on an automatic inflation adjustment. And California does not allow tip credit toward the minimum wage.
 Many other states, including Texas, have failed to raise their minimum wage above the $7.25 national rate.
 And nationwide, the Economic Policy Institute (EPI) reported researchers have calculated a single adult without children needs an average of $17 to $25+ per hour to cover basic subsistence needs. For California, the researchers determined the minimum living wage for a single adult without children averages around $30.48.
 Researchers apparently provide two sets of statistics. The lower of the two is listed as a subsistence wage while the higher listing is an average minimum living wage. And the amounts of subsistence wage vary considerably depending on where you live.
 As examples, subsistence wages were listed for four cities. They are: Chico, CA, approximately $23.50 per hour; Los Angeles, $28.92; rural Missouri, approximately $20, and New York City, about $36.20 per hour.
 Again, each amount listed is for a single adult with no children.
 EPI also has emphasized that wages have failed to stay even close to increases in services and goods produced by U.S. workers. The institute noted worker productivity has nearly doubled (rising 80% to 90%) since the late 1970s — while hourly pay for typical workers grew only 29% to 33%.
 Low wages, however, is only one of the affordability issues facing workers and families. So voters are demanding that Democrats not only end the war and tariffs, they want funds restored for Medicaid, the Biden-era child tax credits, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that helps feed low-income families.
 A HOUSING SOLUTION 
 Land is expensive. Construction is expensive. And the days of couples in their 20s and 30s being able to afford homes of 1,400 to 2,000 square feet are in the past.
 The demand is there; but wages and salaries aren’t there.
 Our young adults have been spoiled by their parents raising them in homes larger than what their adult children can afford. And it’s because the wages and salaries available to them simply have not been climbing nearly enough to meet today’s expenses.
 So I believe one workable answer lies in construction similar to what was necessary for returning soldiers and young families after World War Two. It was the age of multiplexes in the scramble to build affordable homes quickly.
 I grew up in a duplex owned by my parents. And after my first apartment rental, I rented one of the middle homes in a fourplex built for returning GIs. There was no garage — just an off-street parking pad in the front, plus a small yard in the back.
 And my first mortgaged home was a duplex with a rear yard — before I graduated into that most-in-demand single family home.
 Some duplexes, like the one my parents owned, had as many as 3 and 4 floors — if you count unfinished basements and attics.
 As time went by, my father enlarged our basement by excavating under the back porch — to provide a recreation room with stairs to an outside entrance. We had a meeting area with a dartboard, table tennis and an old pinball machine. A pool table was a wish that didn’t materialize.
 We also had a small rear yard and a garage that was accessible via an alley. Many neighborhoods had alleys back then.
 I believe growing up in a neighborhood of family-owned multiplexes was considerably better than living in multi-story apartment buildings — one of the solutions being pushed today.
 Isn’t ground-level entry to your home more preferable than an apartment on a second or third floor, or higher?
 It’s time for a realistic home-ownership approach to today’s affordability situations. And multiplexes for beginning families should be given a priority consideration for the more wholesome outdoor access they provide.
 State and local governments, and NIMBYs, are long overdue to accept and promote multiplex housing.
 Darrell Berkheimer is a retired journalist living in Grass Valley. He has nine books available through Amazon Books, and at SPD. His two Essays books include nearly 120 columns published by The Union, plus a variety of travel and photo essays. Contact him at mtmrnut@yahoo.com .
